headline: How many famous stock-market patterns survive common filters for very small firms?
title: Replicating Anomalies
note: Using standardized construction choices and common breakpoints, the researchers found that many published anomaly variables did not clear the selected statistical threshold.

headline: Can records of European settler deaths explain today's income gaps?
title: The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation
note: The paper used historical settler mortality as an instrument for present-day institutions. A published comment challenged the assignment and comparability of mortality observations. The original authors disputed the critique. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.102.6.3059 https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.102.6.3077

headline: Do taxi drivers go home early when business is unusually good?
title: Labor Supply of New York City Cabdrivers: One Day at a Time
note: The authors inferred that some drivers stopped once they hit an earnings target. Hours and realized earnings per hour came from trip records rather than an assigned wage. Later work using a larger sample found different labor-supply responses. https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/130/4/1975/1916077

headline: Can the last two digits of your Social Security number sway what you bid for wine?
title: “Coherent Arbitrariness”: Stable Demand Curves Without Stable Preferences
note: Participants considered prices derived from their Social Security numbers before stating maximum bids for goods, including wine. The reported association was between the induced anchor and lab valuations.

headline: Does the stock market need a nap after the clocks change?
title: Losing Sleep at the Market: The Daylight Saving Anomaly
note: The authors compared returns after clock-change weekends with returns after ordinary weekends. They reported lower returns after the clocks changed and proposed disrupted sleep as an explanation. An American Economic Review comment challenged the robustness of the clock-change result. The original authors published a reply. https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v92y2002i4p1251-1256.html https://doi.org/10.1257/00028280260344795

headline: Do shorter winter days scare investors off risk?
title: Winter Blues: A SAD Stock Market Cycle
note: The authors linked the length of daylight to stock returns across markets. They proposed that seasonal affective disorder changes investors’ appetite for risk. Kelly and Meschke reexamined the result and reported no consistent connection between stock returns and the proposed seasonal-depression mechanism. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378426609003240

headline: Can famous stock-market forecasts beat a historical average on data they have never seen?
title: A Comprehensive Look at The Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction
note: The study compared historical forecasting variables against a running historical-average benchmark. Previously reported in-sample predictability often did not translate to superior out-of-sample forecasts.

headline: Does handing someone a mug suddenly make it worth more to them?
title: Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem
note: In exchange experiments, mug owners asked for more to sell than buyers offered. Later research found that procedural details could alter observed exchange asymmetries. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.4.1449

headline: Will the second-poorest player give money upward to avoid falling into last place?
title: “Last-Place Aversion”: Evidence and Redistributive Implications
note: In a lab allocation game the authors reported patterns consistent with protecting one's rank near the bottom. The lab project's selected contrast did not meet its replication criterion. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1093/qje/qjt035/

headline: Do stock-return patterns shrink once a paper tells everyone about them?
title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
note: The authors compared returns to published predictors in-sample, outside the original period before publication, and after publication. Average returns were lower in the two later segments. The publication comparison was observational.

headline: Do people actually score worse on cognitive tests just before payday?
title: Poverty and Economic Decision-Making: Evidence from Changes in Financial Resources at Payday
note: The study assigned low-income participants to complete tasks before or after payday. It detected no payday-related difference in cognitive performance. This tested short-term changes in cash on hand, a different exposure from the financial scenarios and harvest timing studied in the earlier Science paper. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1238041

headline: Did moving-average trading rules work beyond the stock history used to find them?
title: Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns
note: The original analysis tested technical rules on historical Dow data. A later analysis examined a larger search universe with a data-snooping adjustment and tested the rules on later observations. https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00163

headline: Did betting on low-risk stocks work partly because of the way researchers measured risk?
title: Betting against beta
note: The original paper documented returns to a long-short factor based on estimated market beta and interpreted them with a leverage-constraints model. A later study challenged aspects of factor construction and interpretation. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X21002051

headline: Does expecting more pay make you work longer even when the pay rule is unchanged?
title: Reference Points and Effort Provision
note: Participants could stop a real-effort task and receive either task earnings or a fixed payment determined by chance. The original reported more work under a higher fixed-payment possibility. A later replication did not recover the focal effect under its criterion. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1257/aer.101.2.470/

headline: Can expecting to keep an object make you less willing to trade it?
title: Expectations as Endowments: Evidence on Reference-Dependent Preferences from Exchange and Valuation Experiments
note: The experiments varied expectations about keeping an assigned object and reported changes in trade or valuation. The focal result did not meet the later replication criterion. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1093/qje/qjr034/

headline: Can a promise of higher pay later keep workers from slacking now?
title: Deferred Compensation in Multiperiod Labor Contracts: An Experimental Test of Lazear's Model
note: The study tested labor contracts in a multi-period game. Ability to commit to later pay was one experimental condition. A later replication did not recover the selected contrast under its replication criterion. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1257/aer.101.2.819/

headline: Did charging late parents make more of them show up late?
title: A Fine is a Price
note: In an Israeli daycare field experiment, late pickups increased after a small fine was introduced. A follow-up in a tax experiment examined how contingent the outcome was on the design. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.irle.2020.105906

headline: Did fast-food employment fall after New Jersey raised the minimum wage?
title: Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania
note: The original restaurant survey did not find a relative employment decline. A payroll-data comment argued for a different result. The authors' reply presented additional payroll-based comparisons. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.90.5.1362 https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.90.5.1397

headline: Do stocks with easier-to-pronounce names rise faster after listing?
title: Predicting short-term stock fluctuations by using processing fluency
note: The paper combined an experiment on judgments with analyses of newly listed stocks and ticker pronounceability. The reported relationship varied by time horizon. A later study used a different name-fluency measure. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X13001141

headline: Do generous participants keep giving when the experiment also lets them take money?
title: On the Interpretation of Giving in Dictator Games
note: Giving fell when the game allowed taking from the other person as well as giving. The change in the menu altered the observed generosity in the game.

headline: Does a surprise raise buy a whole day's extra effort or only a few hours?
title: Putting Behavioral Economics to Work: Testing for Gift Exchange in Labor Markets Using Field Experiments
note: In two short-term jobs, unexpected higher pay elicited an early productivity response that faded later in the work period.

headline: Can paying a tiny amount make people do worse than paying them nothing?
title: Pay Enough or Don't Pay at All
note: In the reported tasks, including a test and a donation-collection exercise, low incentives could produce lower performance than no personal pay. Higher pay outperformed lower pay within paid conditions.

headline: Do CEOs get a raise when oil prices rise even though they did not set the price?
title: Are CEOs Rewarded for Luck? The Ones Without Principals Are
note: The authors isolated company-performance fluctuations tied to external factors and related them to chief executive pay. Estimated pay for favorable shocks varied with measures of corporate governance.

headline: Does a sunny morning give the stock market a lift?
title: Good Day Sunshine: Stock Returns and the Weather
note: The authors matched morning weather in the cities hosting 26 countries’ main stock exchanges with daily index returns. Sunnier mornings were associated with higher returns.

headline: The national team lost. Is the stock market next?
title: Sports Sentiment and Stock Returns
note: The authors compared international sports results with national stock indices. After a country lost a World Cup knockout match, the average next-day return was 0.49 percentage points below the benchmark.

headline: How much value does Santa destroy each Christmas?
title: The Deadweight Loss of Christmas
note: Students estimated what their Christmas gifts had cost and what those gifts were worth to them. The author used the gap to estimate how much value was lost through gift giving.

headline: Sell in May and sit out the market until Halloween?
title: The Halloween Indicator, “Sell in May and Go Away”: Another Puzzle
note: The authors split the trading year in two. In 36 of the 37 markets they examined, average returns from November through April exceeded those from May through October.

headline: Want to hire a profitable trader? Measure his fingers?
title: Second-to-fourth digit ratio predicts success among high-frequency financial traders
note: The researchers measured the fingers of 44 male traders in London. Within that group, traders whose index fingers were shorter relative to their ring fingers had higher long-term trading profits.

headline: Can the Super Bowl winner predict whether the stock market rises?
title: An Examination of the Super Bowl Stock Market Predictor
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Want tenure in economics? An A surname might help.
title: What's in a Surname? The Effects of Surname Initials on Academic Success
note: At the top ten US economics departments, tenured faculty were more likely to have surnames near the start of the alphabet. The authors pointed to the discipline’s practice of listing coauthors alphabetically.

headline: Can Twitter's mood predict the Dow Jones?
title: Twitter mood predicts the stock market
note: The authors extracted mood scores from Twitter posts and reported improved forecasting performance for the Dow Jones Industrial Average in their dataset.

headline: Can a trader’s morning spit predict his day’s profits?
title: Endogenous steroids and financial risk taking on a London trading floor
note: Researchers collected saliva from male traders on a London trading floor. On days when a trader had higher morning testosterone, he also tended to earn more.

headline: Can the shape of a CEO's face predict company performance?
title: A Face Only an Investor Could Love: CEOs’ Facial Structure Predicts Their Firms’ Financial Performance
note: The paper relates CEOs' facial proportions to company financial performance.

headline: How much is the company worth? Check the CEO’s golf calendar.
title: FORE! An Analysis of CEO Shirking
note: The authors used rounds of golf as a measure of CEO leisure. The most frequent golfers ran firms with lower operating performance and lower valuations.

headline: Meant to buy MCIC. Bought MCI instead?
title: Massively Confused Investors Making Conspicuously Ignorant Choices (MCI–MCIC)
note: The author compared two securities with similar ticker symbols. Their short-term returns, trading volume and volatility moved together, a pattern he attributed to investors mixing them up.

headline: What was a dot-com name worth during the internet boom?
title: A Rose.com by Any Other Name
note: The authors tracked firms that announced a switch to an internet-related name. Over the ten days surrounding the announcement, their shares gained about 74% more than the benchmark.

headline: Do CEOs with deeper voices run bigger companies?
title: Voice pitch and the labor market success of male chief executive officers
note: The authors relate male CEO voice pitch to firm size and compensation.

headline: Is a lucky stock code bad luck for investors?
title: Superstition and Financial Decision Making
note: Among newly listed Chinese companies, the authors found more lucky numerical stock codes than chance would predict. Stocks with those codes had lower benchmark-adjusted returns after listing.

headline: Should US investors avoid the World Cup?
title: Exploitable Predictable Irrationality: The FIFA World Cup Effect on the U.S. Stock Market
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
note: The authors reported lower US market returns during World Cup effect periods than comparison periods and proposed a trading strategy.

headline: Does Mercury retrograde knock 3.47% off annualized stock returns?
title: Cultural beliefs and equity prices: Evidence from astrological belief in mercury retrograde
note: The authors reported a lower annualized market return during retrograde periods across 48 countries and interpreted it through investor beliefs.

headline: Should investors check the moon before buying stocks?
title: Are investors moonstruck? Lunar phases and stock returns
note: The authors grouped stock returns from 48 countries by the phase of the moon. Average returns were lower around a full moon than around a new moon.

headline: Can the mood of music listeners predict next week's stock returns?
title: Music sentiment and stock returns around the world
note: Researchers used the mood of music streamed by listeners as a sentiment indicator. They reported positive contemporaneous return associations and negative next-week associations.

headline: Do other golfers play worse when Tiger Woods shows up?
title: Quitters Never Win: The (Adverse) Incentive Effects of Competing with Superstars
note: The author compared professional tournaments with and without Woods. When he played, the other golfers averaged about 0.2 strokes more in the first round.

headline: Does reminding people of their religion change how much they chip in?
title: Religious Identity and Economic Behavior
note: Researchers experimentally made religious identity salient. They reported contrasting effects on public-good contributions by religious affiliation. These estimates come from a laboratory contribution task.

headline: Did a much larger set of taxi logs support the idea that drivers quit after hitting a daily target?
title: Why You Can't Find a Taxi in the Rain and Other Labor Supply Lessons from Cab Drivers
note: The larger trip dataset generally showed positive labor-supply responses to better earnings opportunities, with heterogeneity across drivers. The result challenges a simple daily income-target account.

headline: Do economics students cooperate less after studying economics?
title: Does Studying Economics Inhibit Cooperation?
note: The authors compared students' responses and behavior across tasks and discussed both education and selection. A published response challenged the generalization and examined other measures of cooperation. https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.10.1.177

headline: Can framing the same poetry reading turn someone's desired fee into a bid to attend?
title: Tom Sawyer and the Construction of Value
note: Participants first contemplated either paying for or being paid to hear a poetry reading. Initial framing changed how they subsequently valued the experience.

headline: Do gym members pay more for their workouts by choosing a monthly plan?
title: Paying Not to Go to the Gym
note: Health-club attendance and plan records showed that many flat-fee subscribers paid more per actual visit than an available pay-per-visit alternative. The paper examined overconfidence about future attendance as an explanation.

headline: Can changing only the name on a résumé change whether an employer calls back?
title: Are Emily and Greg More Employable Than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination
note: The correspondence experiment randomized racially distinctive names across fictitious résumés and compared callbacks. The measured outcome was the employer's initial response to the application.

headline: Does switching to winner-takes-all pay change men's and women's maze-solving scores differently?
title: Performance in Competitive Environments: Gender Differences
note: The lab experiment compared piece-rate and tournament compensation for maze solving. The authors reported different performance responses by gender under the experimental competition rules.

headline: Does trading experience make people less reluctant to give up an item?
title: Does Market Experience Eliminate Market Anomalies?
note: Field experiments at trading venues reported smaller exchange asymmetries among more experienced participants. A later study directly examined exogenous market experience. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.101.3.313

headline: Can assigning strangers to teams change how they split money?
title: Group Identity and Social Preferences
note: In assigned-group lab games, participants treated in-group and out-group counterparts differently on some allocation measures. The experiment measured choices in the assigned group setting.

headline: How much do backtests miss when they drop the last return of failed stocks?
title: The Delisting Bias in CRSP Data
note: The study found that returns associated with negative delistings were often missing in the historical data, and used additional information to assess the magnitude of omitted losses.

headline: Did last quarter's winners keep beating last quarter's losers?
title: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency
note: Portfolios ranked by past returns showed positive momentum over several intermediate holding periods in the historical sample. The evidence concerns portfolios built by those ranking rules.

headline: Did stock returns jump just before market holidays?
title: High Stock Returns before Holidays: Existence and Evidence on Possible Causes
note: This historical study found higher mean returns before market holidays. Later out-of-sample research reported that the premium was largely concentrated in small firms. https://www.emerald.com/cfr/article-abstract/13/3-4/531/1326451/The-Pre-Holiday-Premium-of-Ariel-1990-Has-Largely

headline: Can Google searches for a ticker forecast a short-lived price rise?
title: In Search of Attention
note: The study used search volume as an investor-attention proxy and related spikes to short-run price increases and subsequent reversal. Search volume and returns were measured from observed data.

headline: Can the tone of a newspaper column predict tomorrow's market moves?
title: Giving Content to Investor Sentiment: The Role of Media in the Stock Market
note: The analysis measured pessimistic language in a Wall Street Journal column and found associations with near-term price pressure and subsequent reversal. Text tone was a measured proxy for sentiment.

headline: Can a county's religious composition predict demand for lottery-like stocks?
title: Religious Beliefs, Gambling Attitudes, and Financial Market Outcomes
note: The study used local religious composition as a proxy for attitudes toward gambling and related it to financial outcomes. Area-level composition and personal beliefs are distinct measurements.

headline: Can the price of a closed-end fund measure investors' mood?
title: Investor Sentiment and the Closed-End Fund Puzzle
note: The authors interpreted common movement in closed-end fund discounts using an investor-sentiment account and tested predictions relating discounts to other outcomes.

headline: What happened after Robinhood users crowded into the same stocks?
title: Attention-Induced Trading and Returns: Evidence from Robinhood Users
note: Stocks experiencing intense Robinhood buying subsequently showed lower abnormal returns on average. The paper used platform data and investigated the role of app-driven attention.

headline: Did the households that traded the most do the worst after costs?
title: Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors
note: Brokerage records showed worse net returns among the most active trading households. Comparisons came from one discount brokerage over its observed period.

headline: Did men trade more and lose more to trading costs?
title: Boys Will Be Boys: Gender, Overconfidence, and Common Stock Investment
note: Men traded more frequently in the brokerage records and incurred larger return reductions from trading. Overconfidence was the proposed explanation rather than a directly observed account characteristic.

headline: Do investors sell winners quickly while holding on to losing stocks?
title: Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?
note: The study compared realized gains and losses with paper gains and losses in brokerage accounts. It found a greater propensity to sell winners outside a year-end tax-related exception.

headline: Can a bubble form when traders cannot buy a share and sell it on to someone else?
title: Nonspeculative Bubbles in Experimental Asset Markets: Lack of Common Knowledge of Rationality vs. Actual Irrationality
note: The researchers still observed prices departing from the benchmark in a laboratory design that ruled out resale speculation for individual traders.

headline: Can changing the rules bring a bubble back even for experienced traders?
title: Thar She Blows: Can Bubbles Be Rekindled with Experienced Subjects?
note: After subjects gained experience, the experiment changed the market environment and observed renewed bubbles. The later economics replication project reported success on its selected contrast. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1257/aer.98.3.924/

headline: Can January's stock market predict the Super Bowl winner?
title: Exploring a market curiosity: an examination of the Super Bowl Indicator
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can storms on the Sun predict stock returns on Earth?
title: Playing the field: Geomagnetic storms and international stock markets
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Working Paper 2003-5
note: The working paper reported that unusually high geomagnetic activity in the preceding week predicted lower stock returns in several markets.

headline: Do Chinese investors earn less in their own zodiac year?
title: Impact of perceived unlucky years on investment performance: Evidence from Chinese cultural beliefs
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can the size of a CEO's signature reveal bad investments?
title: Narcissism is a bad sign: CEO signature size, investment, and performance
note: CEO signature size is used as a narcissism proxy in a study of investment and financial results.

headline: Born in June or July? What are your odds of becoming CEO?
title: The relative-age effect and career success: Evidence from corporate CEOs
note: June and July birthdays were underrepresented among the CEOs in the sample. The authors suggested that children born in those months might have been among the youngest in their class.

headline: Do unlucky dates produce better stock returns in Asian markets?
title: Superstitions and stock trading: some new evidence
venue: Journal of the Asia Pacific Economy
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Would you buy a stock called MOO?
title: Would a stock by any other ticker smell as sweet?
venue: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
note: The authors picked out memorable ticker symbols, including MOO and LUV. From 1984 to 2005, the stocks in that group earned higher average daily returns than the market as a whole.

headline: Can a CEO's face tell investors how risky a firm is?
title: The face of risk: CEO facial masculinity and firm risk
note: The paper links CEO facial width-to-height ratios to firm risk measures.

headline: Can a CEO's facial proportions predict tax avoidance?
title: Do more masculine-faced CEOs reflect more tax avoidance? Evidence from Indonesia
note: The researchers measure facial ratios and relate them to corporate tax avoidance measures.

headline: Do lucky digits in Taiwanese ticker codes earn higher returns?
title: Lucky issuance: The role of numerological superstitions in irrational return premiums
note: The authors compared returns of Taiwanese listed firms grouped by digits considered lucky or unlucky in their stock codes.

headline: Do investors avoid stock prices that end in the number four?
title: The impact of numerical superstition on the final digit of stock price
venue: North American Journal of Economics and Finance
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does a house sell for more if its address ends in 8?
title: Superstition in the Housing Market
note: The authors analyzed nearly 117,000 home sales. They found a discount for addresses ending in 4 and a premium for those ending in 8 in neighborhoods with a higher share of Chinese residents or in repeat sales.

headline: Do stock markets make fast profits during Ramadan?
title: Fast profits: Investor sentiment and stock returns during Ramadan
note: Daily equity returns in 14 predominantly Muslim countries were compared across calendar periods; the paper reported higher returns during Ramadan.

headline: Can an aviation disaster move the entire stock market?
title: Sentiment and stock prices: The case of aviation disasters
note: The authors reported market-wide price declines after aviation disasters followed by a price reversal, attributing the pattern to investor sentiment.

headline: Does the Super Bowl affect stocks near the competing teams?
title: Sentiment and Stock Returns: Anticipating a Major Sporting Event
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can the morning weather report beat a world stock index?
title: Global weather-based trading strategies
note: The authors used weather variables to construct trading signals and reported higher returns for a weather-based hedge strategy than a world equity index in their test sample.

headline: Do cloudy days depress Taiwanese stock market returns?
title: Are stock market returns related to the weather effects? Empirical evidence from Taiwan
venue: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does a cloudy morning make traders sell rather than buy?
title: Weather and intraday patterns in stock returns and trading activity
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can the air outside predict the stock market?
title: Ambient particulate air pollution and daily stock market returns and volatility in 47 cities worldwide
note: The authors examined time-series associations between local particulate pollution and daily stock market measures across 47 cities.

headline: Can the temperature outside predict stock market returns?
title: Stock market returns: A note on temperature anomaly
note: The authors studied daily temperature and stock returns, interpreting their reported relationship in terms of investor mood.

headline: Does the temperature outside change the way retail investors trade?
title: Temperature and trading behaviours
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does the weather change market liquidity and trading volume?
title: Intraday analyses on weather-induced sentiment and stock market behavior
venue: The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does an unusually hot or cold day change a firm's stock returns?
title: Extreme Temperatures and Firm-Level Stock Returns
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Someone died next door. Does my apartment lose value?
title: Spillovers in Prices: The Curious Case of Haunted Houses
note: The authors tracked Hong Kong homes where an unnatural death had occurred, along with properties nearby. They reported discounts for neighboring units that grew larger the closer a unit was to the site of the death.

headline: Can a few extra inches of height predict a bigger salary?
title: The effect of physical height on workplace success and income: preliminary test of a theoretical model
note: Four samples were used to estimate the relationship between height and income after adjusting for selected demographic variables.

headline: Is there a salary premium for being rated attractive?
title: Beauty and the Labor Market
note: The authors analyzed earnings and observer ratings of physical appearance, reporting wage differences associated with those ratings.

headline: Does a graduate's height or BMI predict starting salary?
title: Attractive Physical Appearance vs. Good Academic Characteristics: Which Generates More Earnings?
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.
